pr_body:
This is complete rework how typed arrays do function. In terms of interactions now typed arrays act like packed arrays do.

No more implicit conversions between arrays on assigns.
```gdscript
var ints: Array[int] = [1]
var floats: Array[float] = ints # will not work
# same as you cannot do this:
var ints := PackedInt64Array()
var floats: PackedFloat64Array = ints
```

`Array` (without a parameter) for typed arrays is what `Variant` is for other types. It is possible to assign typed array to assignable (variable/parameter/constant) with type of basic array and it is possible to do the opposite, but later fails if types do not match.
```gdscript
var ints: Array[int] = [1]
var basic: Array = ints
ints = basic

var floats: Array[float] = [1.0]
basic = floats
ints = basic # runtime error because assigned is Array[float] and not Array[int]

basic = [2]
ints = basic # runtime error because assigned is Array and not Array[int]
```

Explicit inference no longer tries to guess what element type an array has, it will be typed as basic one. 
```gdscript
var infer := [1, 2, 3] # type is Array, not Array[int]
```

Typed arrays in constants now work properly.
```gdscript
const ints: Array[int] = [1] # value now is really Array[int]
```

There is no implicit conversions between arrays, but there is for array literals. In all examples above literal on right side is a usual array literal, but it gets converted during analysis to be of proper type and fails if it is impossible to do. It applies to variable/parameters/constants initializers, assignments, returns, arguments and casts:
```gdscript
var ints: Array[int] = [1] # init
ints = [2] # assign
var floats := [3.0] as Array[float] # cast
var make_bools = func() -> Array[bool]: return [true] # return
func pass_strings(strings: Array[String]): pass # this is a member function, lambdas are untyped
pass_strings(['ok']) # arg 
```

`typed_assign` now does only one thing - replaces contents of an array with contents from another with conversions if needed. It is also renamed to simple `assign`.
```gdscript
var ints: Array[int] = [1]
var floats: Array[float] = []
floats.assign(ints)
```

Fixed `resize` not using `resize_zeroed` and not initializing new elements in typed arrays. This was leading to memory corruptions and crashes.

In `VariantInterals::initialize` add missing initailization for `Projection` and `Color` (alpha needs to be set at 1).

Added serialization/deserialization of typed arrays. Though it does not handle custom classes at the moment.

Fixed undo/redo for packed arrays, for some reason they were excluded from that before.

Changed editors for arrays/dictionaries a little - no need to do recursively duplicate them on each rerender, do it only when value is about to be modified.

Fixed default values for arrays/dictionaries not showing in editor.

Fixed `GDScriptInstance::set` not converting values when setters involved.

Related issues:

Fixes #55916 (about constants).
Fixes #56389 (about documentation).

pr_comments:
Rebased and fixed two more problems (one only partially) regarding constant arrays.

```gdscript
func _ready():
  const x: Array[ int ] = [ 1 ]
  var y := x[ 0 ] # before: error, after: inferring works
  x.push_back( '1' )
  print( x ) # before: [1, "1"], after: [1]
```

First, inference on constant arrays was not working because of misplaced line in subscript reduction that was setting result type to Variant even if type was known. In attribute subscript the line was fixed in #64046, but index was left as it was.

Second, partially fixes #68978, the problem was that `reduced_value` of constant arrays was an array on which `set_typed` was not called. Fixed only partially because while now it works for builtin types properly for custom scripts it seems not because `script_type` reference is not resolved yet...

Two more commits related to constants. 

First makes all constants (local, member, outer, base) to use `resolve_constant` to resolve the type. Locals were already using it. Members were using copy-paste version of it. Outer/Base ones were only reducing an initializer, but it is insufficient since for constant parameterized arrays a declared type is important. (Also removed useless `all_is_constant` variable from `const_fold_array`/`const_fold_dictionary`.)

Second builds on it and clears up some current problems with deepness/flatness of constants. Now if you index constant by another constant a result is not a constant unless it is happening during constants resolution. Some examples of the problem is shown here - #62680. As I understand though there is a discussion about whenever or not make constants truly deep. Have no problem dropping that commit, but if constants will go as flat into version 4 then this at least makes it work properly.

Fixed another thing about arrays (not connected to literals or constants) - typed assigns. Right now if element types are somewhat compatible a destination array just references a source array losing its own type in a process.

```gdscript
class A: pass
class B extends A: pass

func _ready():
  var b: Array[ B ] = [ B.new() ]
  var a: Array[ A ] = b # before: a references b, becomes Array[ B ], after: a copies b contents
  a.push_back( A.new() )
  a.push_back( B.new() )
  print( b.size() ) # before: 2, now: 1
  print( a.size() ) # before: 2, now: 3
  check( a ) # before: error, now: works

func check( a: Array[ A ] ) -> void: print( 'check' )
```

To make it correct array `a` should copy contents of array `b` and maintain its own type info.

By the way, initial commit fixes #69198 and #67889.
You need to squash the commits as required by our pipeline (https://docs.godotengine.org/en/latest/community/contributing/pr_workflow.html#modifying-a-pull-request).
Oh, I was doing that initially, but then it grew and I assume became harder to review in a single commit. Also I assume that third commit might be dropped (about flatness/deepness of constants).

Fixed #63502, now default values should work properly with params of array type.

Also made array assign be used when typed array is assigned to non-typed one. In `Array::_assign` such case was handled by copying contents, but typed array assign was used only if a destination array had an element type and presence of element type in a source array was ignored (so before typed->untyped was just changing reference, now it copies contents).

Amended last commit, is it ok? Or should I still squash the commits into one?

Made changes to `update_array_literal_element_type` and `is_type_compatible`.

In `update_array_literal_element_type` made sure to guard against ending up with Variant in an element type. There was no such guards before but `has_container_element_type` implies that it is not Variant if present.

In `is_type_compatible` reflect that arrays with two different but compatible types are only compatible if implicit conversion is allowed. And same with an assignment of a typed to an untyped array.

Added a test.

After I made `is_type_compatible` to use exact equality for element types when no implicit conversion is allowed I've encountered bugs when a class type was not equal to the same class type. Turns out in `is_type_compatible` compassion was done by equating `fqcn`s (fully-qualified class name) while `==` operator only checked equality of pointers to `ClassNode`, but it seems like the same class may have multiple `ClassNode` instances pointing to it (hence, I assume, why `is_type_compatible` used `fqcn`). So I added comparison of `fqcn` in `==` operator for classes types. Right now `fqcn` is a `String`, but is there anything preventing it from being `NodePath`?

Fixed another major thing about array assigns.
```gdscript
var first: Array[ A ] = []
var second: Array[ A ] = first
var value: Variant = A.new()
second = [ value ]
print( first.size() ) # before: 1, after: 0
print( second.size() ) # 1
```
Currently `Array::_assign` changes contents of an array it points to if there is a type mismatch instead of creating new array and properly copying contents. Here `second` starts referencing the same array as `first` as they have the same type, but during the assignment of the array literal which is `Array[Variant]` instead of trying to creating new `Array[A]` from what is given it simply replaces an underlying vector of the array it already has.

Rebased to resolve conflicts. Fixed one regression from #68747 and another preexisting problem that was revealed there.

The small regression is on [this line](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f1f8d74b0f0790caab2f8d82ce2130c79b2aaf63/core/variant/array.cpp#L219): when changing the call from `validate` to `validate_object` `Variant::NIL` type was forgotten.

The thing revealed: there were additions of lines in [`GDScriptAnalyzer::is_type_compatible`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f1f8d74b0f0790caab2f8d82ce2130c79b2aaf63/modules/gdscript/gdscript_analyzer.cpp#L4186-L4187) and [`Array::_assign`](
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f1f8d74b0f0790caab2f8d82ce2130c79b2aaf63/core/variant/array.cpp#L206-L207) to make exceptions for `String`/`StringName` pair. In fact those lines are not needed.

In `_assign` it showed that currently there is no check if arrays have types of convertible primitives. Meaning that before you could not assign `Array[float]` to `Array[int]` (where a conversion was allowed). There was no problem converting an array of floats to ints if an array of floats was typed as a simple array of variants, in that case each element would have been checked one by one if they are convertible to int, but no luck if you typed things properly. Now this case is handled.

In `is_type_compatible` [nested call](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f1f8d74b0f0790caab2f8d82ce2130c79b2aaf63/modules/gdscript/gdscript_analyzer.cpp#L4203) to resolve if element types of arrays are compatible passes false to `p_allow_implicit_conversion` when it should pass the current value down - if an implicit conversion allowed then arrays with convertible types should be ok, if not then not.

Squashed into one, removed commit about deepness/flatness of constants, added assertions about previous comment fixes.

Also made code structure of `resolve_parameter` match those of variables and constants (done to properly infer a param type when an array literal is a default value). 

While doing this I noticed that `resolve_variable`, `resolve_constant`, `resolve_parameter` and code for resolving member variables and constants are the samish (it just deciding on a type based on an initializer and an annotated type). It looks like copy-paste with sometimes changed names and missing assertions here and there (I assume because with time people add changes here and there but don't know that the code is duplicated in other places). It looks doable to unify that under a single function (which I did here but only for member constants and local constants). But that just a note, will not do that in this PR.

Rebased to fix a conflict with #69992 which was fixing `is_type_compatible` like was written in [the before last comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/69248#issuecomment-1345485373). Interestingly it also fixed an inconsistency between member and local constant resolutions but missed the fact that `resolve_parameter` has [the same problem](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/db6976eed4c59b3a320cb26938898c732ef6b7ca/modules/gdscript/gdscript_analyzer.cpp#L1755). This is an example for the last comment. Added missing `true` to `is_type_compatible` check in `resolve_parameter`.

Note on topic of arrays: currently plus operator returns an untyped array even if two arrays involved are typed and have the same type.

Does this fix the following bug/issue?

```gdscript
extends Control

var _buttons: Array[Button]

func _ready() -> void:
    # Error: Trying to assign a typed array with an array of different type.
    _buttons = [$Button1, $Button2, $Button3]
```

While in some other cases this works:

```gdscript
extends Control

var _ints: Array[int]

func _ready() -> void:
    _ints = [1, 2, 3]
```

This is probably because the type is guessed, although it is not explicitly specified.

```gdscript
print([1, 2, 3].get_typed_builtin()) # 0 (TYPE_NIL)

var a := [1, 2, 3]
print(a.get_typed_builtin()) # 2 (TYPE_INT) !!!

var b: Array = [1, 2, 3]
print(b.get_typed_builtin()) # 0 (TYPE_NIL)

# Should be the opposite, default is `Array` and `Array[int]` should be explicit.
```

I think we are missing typed array literals (like `Array[int](1, 2, 3)`) to explicitly specify the type without an extra variable. Implicit guessing is confusing and inconsistent.

Sorry for delay in reply, @dalexeev. Added a fix for the shown issue of yours. 

Part of it was fixed before, but typed_assign in Array was still missing a case when you assign from an array of base classes (Node) to an array of extending classes (Button). (It is the same as the one where you assign variants to objects.)

Now it works. Also marked such assignments where a source array cannot be used without conversions/checks as type unsafe.

It seems to me this still needs discussion on what the proper behavior should be. Only then we can say whether the implementation is optimal.

There's also a change in Array that I'm not really convinced. Before it used COW (copy-on-write) which only made a copy if the array changed, but now it's always making a copy. This probably has a performance impact. It's also one thing to be discussed: _when_ (or even _if_) an array should be copied instead of passed by reference.

I think that arrays should not be copied on usual assignment. As was said by @kleonc, arrays are reference types and when you receive an array then you can call `push_back` expecting original one to get element too. In my opinion the only question is convenient explicit api/syntax for converting arrays to other types (by copy).

```gdscript
var subclasses: Array[B] = []
func for_classes(classes: Array[A]): pass
```

What way for a user should there be to pass `subclasses` to `for_classes` (as copy) without too much of a hassle?

Another question is whenever or not inferring should change the type:
```gdscript
var untyped = [1]
var inferred := [2]
```
Should the inferred here be `Array[int]` or be just `Array` (of variants) like `untyped`? It can cause problems to have `Array[int]` if you plan to use it in places that expect just `Array`.

I think what @dalexeev said about syntax might solve both problems:
```gdscript
for_classes(Array[A](subclasses))
inferred_simple := [2]
inferred_int := Array[int]([2])
```

As for copy-on-write - that's sounds like a good idea. But I don't see any trace of it in master... Edit: Found it. It is two levels down in `CowData`. Quite easy to put its use back.

Another major problem with typed arrays is that they are not so much typed, meaning that all of their methods do return/accept same old variants. Array will not be the last parameterized thing in godot, so there is need to think about how to represent type parameters in info. 

Small note (just a note): if braces `{}` were theoretically used for type parameters instead of brackets `[]` (or angle brackets `<>`) then it would have been much easier on parser, since there is no `a{b}` but there is `a[b]` (and `a<b`).

Super exciting!!!! All of it checks out with what we discussed in the meeting, I think!

The only thing that I'd like to discuss a bit more is this one

`var infer := [1, 2, 3] # type is Array, not Array[int]`

Wouldn't it make sense to try to infer the type of the array elements here as well, and if they're not all of the exact same type, default to `Variant` array?

> The only thing that I'd like to discuss a bit more is this one
> 
> `var infer := [1, 2, 3] # type is Array, not Array[int]`

My opinion is that it should just be `Array` (`Array[Variant]`) since GDScript is a dynamic language by default and `Variant` should be used everywhere unless explicitly stated otherwise. `:=` asks us to guess the type, we guess it's an `Array`, but nothing more.

Otherwise, we will have problems such as:

```gdscript
print([1, 2, 3].get_typed_builtin()) # 0 (TYPE_NIL)

var a := [1, 2, 3]
print(a.get_typed_builtin()) # 2 (TYPE_INT) !!!

var b: Array = [1, 2, 3]
print(b.get_typed_builtin()) # 0 (TYPE_NIL)

# Should be the opposite, default is `Array` and `Array[int]` should be explicit.
```

and

```gdscript
var a = [1, 2, 3]
print(a.get_typed_builtin()) # 0 (TYPE_NIL)

var b := [1, 2, 3]
print(b.get_typed_builtin()) # 2 (TYPE_INT) !!!
```

Few things about it:
- By inferring typed array you remove ability to infer basic one (unless it is empty or complete mix). 
- `Array[Class]` and  `Array[SubClass]` are not compatible like before, so it important to get type right.
- Assigning a basic array to a variable with type of a typed array will give an error too.
- Classes may have multiple base classes, it is not exact which one to infer, inferring most specific is an arbitrary choice.
- It complicates codebase.

I do think that decision on whenever or not to make array typed and with which type should be made by a user since there will be consequences. Most people should be ok with a basic array. Have no problem with putting that logic back if that's the consensus though.
I am convinced :) <3

What I am more interested in and what we have not discussed is the implicit conversion of an array literal to typed one.

It can be perceived as somewhat confusing:
```gdscript
var good_int: Array[int] = [0] # this works

var basic = [0]
var bad_int: Array[int] = basic # this does not
```

The reasoning is that when a literal converted we are sure that there are no other references to that array (so nobody can write into it) so it is ok to convert it to typed one.

While some possible confusion is a minus, there is a big plus that you don't have to write `Array[MyClassName]()` anytime you want to create new array for assignment into a variable, passing as an argument or returning from a function. So it will make them much less frictionless to use.

> The reasoning is that when a literal converted we are sure that there are no other references to that array (so nobody can write into it) so it is ok to convert it to typed one.

Maybe the rule could be that implicit conversion only works with a const value? I.e. these two would work:
```gdscript
var good_int: Array[int] = [0] # this works

const CONSTANT = [0]
var good_int2: Array[int] = CONSTANT # this could work

var basic = [0]
var bad_int: Array[int] = basic # this does not
```
That being said it's a fairly theoretical use case, I don't see much value in it. So the current behavior which you outlined is probably sufficient.

Though one use case that may be realistic is something like this:
```gdscript
const TILE_SIZE = 64

var arr: Array[int] = [TILE_SIZE, TILE_SIZE, TILE_SIZE]
```

Last one is already possible. Things inside literal do not have to be literals or constants:
```gdscript
const convertable_const := 0
var matching_var := 1.0
var combined: Array[float] = [convertable_const, matching_var, 2.0, 3] 
print(combined) # [0, 1, 2, 3]
```
Their type must match (`matching_var`, `2.0`) or they can be constants with convertable type (`convertable_const`, `3`).

I finally took some time to review this. Overall seems good to me. The only thing the is off is assignment of untyped -> typed arrays.

In particular, this case gives an error when it should not:
```gdscript
var arr: Array[int];
var i = 0
arr = [i]
```

It says `Cannot have untyped elements in a typed array` in the last line. This is problematic especially for people not using types (GDScript is still dynamically typed by default after all) when interacting with the engine methods or typed third-party addons. Here's an example of potential untyped code giving error, which is a bit contrived since not many things in Godot take typed arrays, but should be enough to illustrate the point:
```gdscript
extends CodeEdit
enum Tokens {
	TK_PERIOD,
}
func _ready(): 
	var token_map = {
		Tokens.TK_PERIOD: ".",
	}
	code_completion_prefixes = [token_map[Tokens.TK_PERIOD]]
```

While changing the dictionary from `var` to `const` works for this, it might not always be an option.

This is more odd considering untyped arrays and typed variant arrays are accepted. In the following image only the last line gives an error. The 3rd line in the function is even marked green:
```gdscript
func add_prefix(x):
	code_completion_prefixes += x
	var arr: Array[String] = code_completion_prefixes + [x]
	code_completion_prefixes = code_completion_prefixes + [x]
	code_completion_prefixes += [x]
```

Essentially, while my previous example gave a parser error, this does not:
```gdscript
var arr: Array[int];
var i = 0
var temp_arr = [i]
arr = temp_arr
```

When this will fail at runtime, but the first should not since it should (try to) create a typed array at runtime. This one even gives all green lines (and also gives error at runtime since the concatenation creates an untyped Array):

```gdscript
var arr: Array[int];
var i = 0
arr = [] + [i]
```

----

In summary, it's giving errors when it shouldn't and there are some cases where green lines are shown when they should not (in particular `typed_array = variant_array`).

I'll also have to discuss with other people the changes in core, especially in VariantParser (and Writer). I think we need to come up with a format that's both good for the documentation and for the serializing (or consider if it's worth splitting those for this case alone). 

For instance, using a number to store the Variant type in the scene file isn't great because it will make files unreadable if the things in `Variant::Type` enum changes order (unlikely to happen until maybe Godot 5, but even then we want to easily port scenes from one version to the next). It should probably write the type as text and have a map to get it back to the actual type, which also helps with documentation.

There's also the case of using `std::optional`. We've been a bit stringent in allowing `std` stuff in core for many reasons. I will have to consult others to see if this is okay.

I can't really comment for the changes in the inspector, I'm not familiar with that code.

> In particular, this case gives an error when it should not

Ok. Removed `Cannot have untyped elements in a typed array`, allowed variants inside literals. It will try to convert now (the same as calling constructor) and error in runtime if fails.

> The 3rd line in the function is even marked green

Ok. Fixed green lines for assignments (though there should be other places like returns and args and so on, can be fixed later).

> using a number to store the Variant type

Unfortunately I do see `Variant::get_type_name` but don't see an inverse function to get a type from a name.

> We've been a bit stringent in allowing `std` stuff in core for many reasons.

Just to be clear for others - `std::optional` usage here is limited to analyzer in GDScript module, is not introduced into core.

presumably #71756 is another one for the list of what this will fix?

(note that enum typed arrays DID work up until beta 11 though).

edit: yes, confirmed the issue I mentioned will be fixed with this PR.

Ok, fixed the shown issue with enum typed arrays.

And relaxed one check for literals taking into account that implicit conversions are now allowed:
```gdscript
var typed_floats: Array[float] = [some_typed_int_var]
```
I think we should merge this PR ASAP, then fix the issues that comes up afterwards. We're imminently close to release release candidates and we need to make sure that this fix is battle-tested.

> > We've been a bit stringent in allowing `std` stuff in core for many reasons.
> 
> Just to be clear for others - `std::optional` usage here is limited to analyzer in GDScript module, is not introduced into core.

It seems there is still resistance among the maintainers (I too have some reservations because of future implications) so I'll ask you to remove the usage, instead use a `bool` return and pass the Variant by reference, or vice-versa. Being in the `core` folder or not does not make much of a difference since everything is in the main codebase and is included by default. 

> Unfortunately I do see `Variant::get_type_name` but don't see an inverse function to get a type from a name.

Yeah, that would need another map from name to type. @reduz suggested looping through the types and matching the name and if performance is an issue cache this statically accessible via a `Variant::get_type_from_name()` method.

There were suggestions of storing the value as if it were a typed constructor (e.g. `Array[int]([1, 2, 3])`) which does look good both on the scene and the docs. In case of custom scripts, they could be saved as `Array[ExtResource("1_w6xmu")]([])`. The VariantParser should be able to detect the `ExtResource(` or `SubResource(`  prefix and treat it accordingly. This is looks to me like the best option.
But I don't think that `Array[int]([1, 2, 3])` will work in generated C++.

> But I don't think that `Array[int]([1, 2, 3])` will work in generated C++.

The bindings generator in godot-cpp can adapt this syntax to generate what is appropriate for C++. The current format in the PR (`Array([1, 2, 3], 2, &"", null)`) is also not valid C++ and would also need an update in the bindings generator.

Is it up to me fix then? What representation should be used for `default_value` in gdextension dump?
`godot-cpp` in another repository and I think [`correct_default_value`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-cpp/blob/ae1afba8d126e2b577ba358f17b2843787f71ef1/binding_generator.py#L2118) would need to be updated.

@bruvzg or @vnen might be able to help fix the godot-cpp bindings generator.
The correct C++ syntax to replace e.g. `Array[RID]([])` would be `TypedArray<RID>()`. There's probably no need to support custom script classes there as they wouldn't be used in the generated API.

True, since it is `TypedArray<T>` it is clearly C++ specific and no changes to gdextension dump is needed.

For docs I kept current format. For that `DocData::get_default_value_string` was added. Since docs do have their own notation for typed arrays anyway and to keep things cleaner.

Besides C++ changes needed in `godot-cpp` repository this one is ready. One small thing though:

I would prefer to rename `typed_assign`. There is no point to keep `typed` in the name now, it is a method in the same category as `push_back`, `append` and `append_array` (not in category of `set_typed`, `is_typed` or `get_typed_builtin`). It does more conversions than those, but the same behavior can be applied to them later.
Now that https://github.com/godotengine/godot-cpp/pull/1018 is merged, this may pass CI after a rebase.

I've rebased the other two PRs. After they are merged will rebase this one and resolve an easy conflict with "constant conversions".

As for rename, I though about which name would be suitable, simply `assign` is ok, but when added later to `Dictionary` maybe too close in name to `merge`. Looked around and I think `copy` is a good one, in C# this is a description for [`Array.Copy`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.array.copy?view=net-7.0):
```
Copies a range of elements in one Array to another Array and performs type casting and boxing as required.
```

Which matches intended behavior of the method.

I rebased and renamed the method. godot-cpp still has a problem because it has [`include/godot_cpp/variant/typed_array.hpp`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-cpp/blob/0f3a0913f100dcd988b538582431d064f46c4e17/include/godot_cpp/variant/typed_array.hpp) which this PR changes, the old one used `typed_assign` in two places which were replace by `_ref` call.

I haven't been able to reconstruct it in a minimal project, but loading a larger project with this PR, the data serialized in many `.tres` and `.tscn` files cannot be loaded (is just being ignored - no error messages). when then re-saving those files, the data is lost.

for instance, a `SpriteFrames` resource plugged into a `AnimatedSprite2D` node is just dropped.
edit: looks like this may be due to something unrelated where the `frames` property has been renamed to `sprite_frames`.

in another case, one of my resources serializes sub resources in a typed array: `@export var arr: Array[MyRes]`, which are all being dropped; the inspector displays an empty array and when saving the resource, the data is lost.

When types are incompatible during setting up an instance from a scene they are silently ignored. That's how it is, yes. So all typed arrays currently serialized in scene files as untyped arrays will be dropped.

One option to soften this is to allow temporary conversion from untyped array to typed one and then later in separate PR disallow such conversion. But it will not guarantee that all untyped arrays were properly resaved and some people skip releases.

And to be clear, after you work with your project and save new arrays (with new format) they are no longer being dropped, only old ones, right?

yes once serialized with the new syntax it's all good.
unfortunately there doesn't seem to be an easy way to identify and fix affected files with a simple search & replace.

real world example from previous to new:

```
conversation = [SubResource("2"), SubResource("3")]
```

```
conversation = Array[Resource("res://generic/resources/dialogue/dialogue_item.gd")]([SubResource("Resource_fvm2a"), SubResource("Resource_qswwh")])
```

edit: in my case it seems I managed to resolve it with some regex. requires very manual attention though not to make incorrect replacements, difficult to automate.

```
conversation = Array[Resource("res://generic/resources/dialogue/dialogue_item.gd")]([SubResource("Resource_fvm2a"), SubResource("Resource_qswwh")])
```

Shouldn't `Resource("res://generic/resources/dialogue/dialogue_item.gd")` also be a `SubResource()` or `ExtResource()` instead of `Resource(path)`?

I haven't tested on a big project myself, but I think we do need to provide an upgrade path for existing scenes. Maybe VariantParser can keep support for the old syntax as additional compatibility code, while VariantWriter would write the new?

> VariantParser can keep support for the old syntax as additional compatibility code

Old syntax is supported and as before produces untyped arrays. `VariantParser` cannot produce typed arrays from `[]` strings, since it doesn't know what type of an array is expected.

Currently in people's scene files all arrays are saved as untyped ones. With this PR there will be no implicit conversion from untyped one to typed one on assignment as before. So incompatible.

> As for rename, I though about which name would be suitable, simply `assign` is ok, but when added later to `Dictionary` maybe too close in name to `merge`. Looked around and I think `copy` is a good one, in C# this is a description for [`Array.Copy`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.array.copy?view=net-7.0):
> 
> ```
> Copies a range of elements in one Array to another Array and performs type casting and boxing as required.
> ```
> 
> Which matches intended behavior of the method.

I don't like the name `copy()` because it sounds to me like it returns a copy of the array (same as `duplicate()`). I think `assign()` makes more sense since you are pretty much performing an assignment operation. Not everyone is familiar with C# to understand the `copy` name right away.

`copy` and `clone` are generic names for such methods in some languages (`clone` does what `duplicate` does in gdscript). C# is a little more relevant than other languages because it is a second officially supported language. For array method name `assign` might work, but for dictionaries (or other types) it might become confusing - `merge` and `assign` (where there is `Object.assign` in js which what `merge` does). `copy` has a required argument with an array to copy so it will be clear that it is not what `duplicate` does.

Note that C#'s `Array.Copy` is a static method which takes in both source and destination arrays (and it's capable of copying only a specific range of elements, possibly starting at specific destination index). A non-static version is [`Array.CopyTo`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.array.copyto?view=net-7.0) which copies the whole array to the specified destination (array + start index). But what's important: these methods actually do perform copying.

In case of "our method" it might end up just assigning the internal array which is copy-on-write and hence actual copying can happen later. So `copy` (or `copy_from` which I think would be a better name) would be a little misleading. On the other hand `assign` does make sense to me, that's pretty much what this method does.

> In case of "our method" it might end up just assigning the internal array which is copy-on-write and hence actual copying can happen later. So copy (or copy_from which I think would be a better name) would be a little misleading.

I don't how it is misleading. It changes contents to match those of source array. That's it. copy-on-write is just an internal optimization/implementation, has nothing to do with behavior.

I see that Python has `copy()` on `List`. So I guess it is no go. I will rename it to `assign`.
Added the same logic to `ResourceLoaderText::load()`.
Thanks!
Congratulations on this huge PR! I know it was a loooooooooot of work with a looooooooot of subtleties, but so very important! Very very excited this got in! :) :) :)

issue_context.title: GDScript 2.0: Function not accepting typed Array with custom classes as a parameter
issue_context.body:
### Godot version

4.0.alpha3

### System information

Window 10

### Issue description

function not accepting custom classes Typed Array as a parameter

### Steps to reproduce

1- Create custom class

**SimpleClass.gd**
```python
class_name SimpleClass

var name

```

2- Create a function that accept 1 param as an array of `SimpleClass`

SomeScript.gd
```python 

func _ready() -> void:
    var simple_class_instance : SimpleClass = SimpleClass.new()
   
    get_array_of_class([simple_class_instance ])

func get_array_of_class(classes : Array[SimpleClass]) -> void:
    print(classes)    
```

You will get an error described as `Cannot convert argument 1 from Array to Array`

### Minimal reproduction project

_No response_
comments:
This seems to exhibit the same behavior as if you were to send a generic array to a typed array:
```gdscript
func _ready():
  var ary = [1, 2, 3]
  test_func(ary)

func test_func(my_ary : Array[int]):
  print(my_ary)
```
`Cannot convert argument 1 from Array to Array`

I did double check and confirmed that even if you make a variable that is statically typed to `Array[SimpleClass]` it still throws this same error, as if the class isn't properly applying the static typing.

What's interesting -
```gdscript
func _ready():
	var ary1 : Array[String] = ["1", "2"]
	var ary2 : Array[RandoClass] = [RandoClass.new()]
	ary1.append(3)
	ary2.append("245")
	print("Array[String] : ", ary1)
	print("Array[RandoClass] : ", ary2)
```
Output: 
Array[String] : [1, 2]
Array[RandoClass] : [[Node:21206401412], 245]

The Array[String] is properly enforcing the static typing, not allowing an `int` to be appended (although - this is silently failing whiich may be a cause for concern)
The Array[RandoClass] however is failing to enforce this static typing, allowing a `String` to be appended

A type mismatch would bring up an error about an invalid argument before even running the code:
```gdscript
func _ready():
  var ary: Array[int] = [1, 2, 3]
  test_func(ary)

func test_func(my_ary : Array[String]):
  print(my_ary)
```
`Parser Error: Invalid argument for "test_func()" function: argument 1 should be Array[String] but is Array[int].`

You don't see this error when dealing with basic variant Array variables.

Tested in 4.0.beta3+ (040f49ed6e71a6e7f23d763c4b56095cbf319ef7):

> ```python
> func _ready() -> void:
>     var simple_class_instance : SimpleClass = SimpleClass.new()
>    
>     get_array_of_class([simple_class_instance ])
> 
> func get_array_of_class(classes : Array[SimpleClass]) -> void:
>     print(classes)    
> ```
>   
> You will get an error described as Cannot convert argument 1 from Array to Array

Works just fine, no error.

---

> What's interesting -
> 
> ```gdscript
> func _ready():
> 	var ary1 : Array[String] = ["1", "2"]
> 	var ary2 : Array[RandoClass] = [RandoClass.new()]
> 	ary1.append(3)
> 	ary2.append("245")
> 	print("Array[String] : ", ary1)
> 	print("Array[RandoClass] : ", ary2)
> ```
> 
> Output:
>Array[String] : [1, 2]
>Array[RandoClass] : [[Node:21206401412], 245]

No longer the case, the second `append` also fails.

---

> ```gdscript
> func _ready():
>   var ary = [1, 2, 3]
>   test_func(ary)
> 
> func test_func(my_ary : Array[int]):
>   print(my_ary)
> ```
>   
> Cannot convert argument 1 from Array to Array

Still the same error (at runtime).

Okay, since my issue is closed, I guess I'll post here as it is obviously connected.
But mine was specifically about constant aspect of it. What I mean is:

This one will fail, yes:
```gd
func _ready(): var ary = [1, 2, 3]; test_func(ary)
```

But this one (properly typed) will pass:
```gd
func _ready(): var ary: Array[int] = [1, 2, 3]; test_func(ary)
```

As will this one (correctly inferred):
```gd
func _ready(): var ary := [1, 2, 3]; test_func(ary)
```

But this one (typed, but constant) will fail again:
```gd
func _ready(): const ary: Array[int] = [1, 2, 3]; test_func(ary)
```

So while the fix for this issue might be about converting `Array[Variant]` to `Array[T]` when passed as an argument. It may actually end up hiding the error in typing of a constant array.

Commenting here with my test case of `map`:

```gdscript
func test(items: Array[int]) -> void: pass

func _ready():
	# Works
	test([1])

	# Doesn't work
	test([1].map(func(x) -> int: x))
```
